metadata.note: The Atlanta - Macon line of Georgia's third railroad: the Monroe Railroad (opened Macon - Forsyth 1838, extended in stages to Griffin by 1843), its successor the Macon and Western (Macon - Atlanta 1846-1872), and the same line under the Central Rail Road and Banking Company of Georgia / Central of Georgia Railway 1873-1946. 1947-1971 is already drawn by cofg-nancy-hanks-ii in central_of_georgia_nancy_hanks.geojson and is not repeated. Every feature draws the same real-traced Norfolk Southern Griffin District geometry (or a piece of it); Rule 4 splits share identical geometry.
metadata.ownership_split: Monroe Railroad (and Banking) Company to 1844 -> sheriff's sale April 1845 and near-year suspension -> Macon and Western Rail Road 1846-1872 (split) -> Central Rail Road and Banking Company of Georgia from 1873 (consolidation approved 1872, formal Jan 7 1873; split) -> Central of Georgia Railway Nov 1 1895 (rename/reorganization of the same company: NOT a split, one colour). Richmond Terminal 1888, receivership 1892-95, Harriman 1907, Illinois Central 1909: stock or court control, not splits.
metadata.omitted: Report block [4] Monroe Railroad Griffin - 'within twenty miles of Atlanta' (towards Jonesboro): drawable NONE - no confirmed opening or passenger year and traction unknown. Block [8] (Atlanta - Macon 1947-1971): already drawn as cofg-nancy-hanks-ii. Blocks [9] Barnesville - Thomaston, [10] Griffin - Newnan - Carrollton and [11] the ETV&G Atlanta - Macon via McDonough: other companies' lines, not this road. The 1840-1842 horse-worked oak-rail extensions Forsyth - Barnesville and Barnesville - Griffin: excluded under Rule 5 (mentioned in notes only).
metadata.horsecar_audit: Not drawn under Rule 5: horse haulage on oak rails Forsyth - Barnesville from fall 1840 until iron arrived in 1841, and Barnesville - Griffin 1841-1842 (Phillips 1908 p.268). Those features start at the first steam year (1841, 1843).
not_yet_sourced: [OPEN] ends: monroe-rr-macon-forsyth, monroe-rr-forsyth-barnesville and monroe-rr-barnesville-griffin end 1844 as the last drawn year, not a known end; whether any Monroe train ran in Jan-Apr 1845 before the sheriff's sale is not established.

The Monroe Railroad stage dates rest on one secondary source, U. B. Phillips (1908), citing 1838-1842 Georgia newspapers not read directly; the Macon Telegraph's 1842 schedule advertisements could move Barnesville - Griffin from 1843 to 1842 and establish explicit passenger carriage north of Forsyth.
The M&W's resumption/through-opening date (Oct 1 1845 vs Sep 4 1846 vs summer 1846) and the exact date the Central began working the trains in 1872-73.
Rule 4/6 at 1895: drawn as one company and colour (rename); the Nancy Hanks layer's metadata argues for a separate pre-1895 company - unresolved at project level.
Rule 4 at 1963 (Southern Railway stock control of the CofG) affects only the existing 1947-1971 cofg-nancy-hanks-ii feature, not this layer.
All headway_min values and avg_speed_kmh values are estimates; no M&W or CofG timetable for 1838-1946 was converted.
The Dixie Flyer (1892-1966) is not attributed to this line; its Atlanta - Macon carrier was not verified.

segments.note: Georgia's third railroad to run trains. First rail laid Oct 9 1838 near the western limits of Macon; locomotive Ocmulgee received Nov 22, the first coach Dec 3, and the first train ran over the road to Forsyth on Dec 10 1838 (Right Way Magazine vol.51 no.5; railga.com; Phillips p.267, citing the Southern Banner of Dec 22 1838). Steam from the first day, so nothing is trimmed under Rule 5. SOURCE CONFLICT, RECORDED: Phillips's summary on p.266 says the road reached Forsyth 'before the end of 1840'; his own detailed account and every other source say 1838, which is used. The 1844 end is an [OPEN] end: it is the last year drawn, NOT a known last day of service. The road was sold at sheriff's sale in April 1845 and trains were suspended for nearly a year in 1845-46 (Phillips pp.264, 269); whether any Monroe train ran in January-April 1845 is not established, so 1845 is withheld. Do not extend without evidence. headway_min is an ESTIMATE (one passenger train each way a day assumed); no Monroe Railroad timetable was seen.
sources: Segment-level: start 1838 per Right Way Magazine (cofga.org), railga.com and Phillips (1908) p.267; end 1844 is an [OPEN] end withheld before the April 1845 sheriff's sale and the 1845-46 suspension (Phillips pp.264, 269); headway NOT SOURCED (estimate)

segments.note: Drawn from 1841, the year iron (and so locomotives) reached Barnesville. Context, not drawn: eleven miles of oak rail were laid in the fall of 1840 and for months the cars were hauled by HORSES from the head of the iron track to Barnesville (Phillips p.268, citing the Southern Recorder of May 19 1840 and Oct 7 1841); those horse-worked months are excluded under Rule 5. The month steam began in 1841 is not established (by Oct 7 1841 at latest). Passenger evidence is indirect: Phillips says 'the cars', and no Barnesville timetable before 1847 was seen; the road opened with a passenger coach, so passenger carriage is the natural reading. The 1844 end is an [OPEN] end: it is the last year drawn, NOT a known last day of service. The road was sold at sheriff's sale in April 1845 and trains were suspended for nearly a year in 1845-46 (Phillips pp.264, 269); whether any Monroe train ran in January-April 1845 is not established, so 1845 is withheld. Do not extend without evidence. headway_min is an ESTIMATE (one passenger train each way a day assumed); no Monroe Railroad timetable was seen.
sources: Segment-level: start 1841 per Phillips (1908) p.268 (Southern Recorder Oct 7 1841); passenger carriage inferred, not directly sourced; end 1844 is an [OPEN] end (Phillips pp.264, 269); headway NOT SOURCED (estimate)

segments.note: Drawn from 1843. Context, not drawn: after iron reached Barnesville in 1841 'an oaken track was laid to Griffin and operated by horse-power', and 'for still another year this patchwork ... policy was continued' (Phillips p.268) - horse working into Griffin 1841-1842, excluded under Rule 5. SOURCE CONFLICT, RECORDED: the UGA Preservation Plan for Griffin says steam locomotives ran by 1842, and railga.com / Wikipedia say the road 'reached Griffin in 1842' without separating horse from steam; 1843 is the inward collapse of the 1842-43 steam bracket. A Macon Telegraph 1842 schedule advertisement could move this to 1842. Same indirect-passenger-evidence caveat as Forsyth - Barnesville. Griffin was laid out in 1840 by the Monroe's president, Gen. Lewis Lawrence Griffin. The Monroe's further extension north of Griffin 'to within twenty miles of Atlanta' is NOT drawn: its opening year and traction are unknown. The 1844 end is an [OPEN] end: it is the last year drawn, NOT a known last day of service. The road was sold at sheriff's sale in April 1845 and trains were suspended for nearly a year in 1845-46 (Phillips pp.264, 269); whether any Monroe train ran in January-April 1845 is not established, so 1845 is withheld. Do not extend without evidence. headway_min is an ESTIMATE (one passenger train each way a day assumed); no Monroe Railroad timetable was seen.

segments.note: The Monroe Railroad was sold at sheriff's sale in April 1845 to Jere Cowles of Macon and reorganized as the Macon and Western by Daniel Tyler of Norwich, Conn. and associates (incorporated Dec 20 1845 per Wikipedia; Phillips has a new charter in 1847). Trains were suspended for nearly a year in 1845-46 (Phillips p.269); the line was completed through to Atlanta in 1846. SOURCE CONFLICT, RECORDED: the Right Way article gives both Oct 1 1845 and Sep 4 1846 for completion, railga.com 'summer of 1846'; 1845 conflicts with the suspension, so 1846 is used. First printed-guide anchor 1847 (Sherman's guide, per Fowler). Atlanta's third railroad and the first rail link from Atlanta to Savannah via the Central at Macon. CIVIL WAR: the Atlanta end was cut c. Sep 1864 - Mar/Apr 1865 (Kilpatrick's raid, the Battle of Jonesboro, Sherman's destruction of eleven miles of rail from Atlanta to near Rough and Ready); the Macon Telegraph of Apr 11 1865 reports freight and passenger trains running regularly again, so no whole year is lost. Ends 1872: consolidation with the Central Rail Road and Banking Company of Georgia was approved by the legislature Aug 24 1872 and the Central's board Nov 26 1872, and formally completed by the M&W Jan 7 1873; the date the Central's men took over train working is not established. headway_min is an ESTIMATE (two trains each way a day assumed), not sourced.
sources: Segment-level: start 1846 per railga.com, Wikipedia and Fowler (Atlanta (MW) station 1846; 1847 Sherman's guide anchor); end 1872 per the consolidation dates in Right Way Magazine (cofga.org); Civil War interruption per the M&W annual report of Dec 1 1865 and the Macon Telegraph of Apr 11 1865; headway NOT SOURCED (estimate)

segments.note: Operated by the Central Rail Road and Banking Company of Georgia after the Macon and Western was consolidated into it (approved Aug 24 1872 by the legislature and Nov 26 1872 by the Central's board; formally completed Jan 7 1873). The Central Rail Road and Banking Company reorganized as the Central of Georgia Railway on Nov 1 1895 - the SAME real company under a new name, running the same trains, so one company and one colour (Rule 4); this segment ends 1894 only so the rename year is not claimed twice. SOURCE CONFLICT, RECORDED: the Nancy Hanks layer's own metadata treats the pre-1895 company as needing a separate colour; the Central of Georgia research file treats 1895 as a rename, not a split, which is followed here. Richmond Terminal stock control from 1888 and the 1892-1895 receivership did not change who ran the trains. Printed anchors inside the span: 1875 Official Guide (Fowler 'y') at East Point, Morrow, Jonesboro, Lovejoy's, Griffin, Orchard Hill, Milner, Barnesville, Goggins, Collier's, Forsyth, Bolingbroke, Summerfield; 1893 Official Guide ('z') at Forest and Smarr's. The first Nancy Hanks, the Central's Atlanta - Savannah flyer, ran over this line in 1892-93. headway_min is an ESTIMATE (two trains each way a day assumed), not sourced.
sources: Segment-level: start 1873 per the consolidation dates in Right Way Magazine (cofga.org); 1875 and 1893 Official Guide anchors per Fowler GA route 40; end 1894 abuts the Nov 1 1895 reorganization (a rename); headway NOT SOURCED (estimate)

segments.note: Central of Georgia Railway, from the Nov 1 1895 reorganization of the Central Rail Road and Banking Company (same company, new name). The CofG's Atlanta - Macon main and its busiest passenger line. Printed anchors inside the span: Fowler's 1901 company timetable (Mitchell Street, Belt Line Junction, McPherson, Mims), 1903 (McDaniel Street), 1915 and 1934 working timetables (Irving). Atlanta's Terminal Station opened 1905, Macon Terminal Station 1916. Harriman (1907), Illinois Central (1909) and Frisco (1956) control were stock purchases with the CofG still running its own trains, so no split. Ends 1946 ONLY to abut the existing cofg-nancy-hanks-ii feature, which draws this same Atlanta - Macon track (as part of Atlanta - Savannah) 1947-1971; passenger service on the line did not end in 1946 - the Oct 1951 Official Guide (Table 1) shows trains 1/2, 3/4, 5/6, 18, 32, 70, 94 and 107/108 on it. headway_min is an ESTIMATE (about six trains each way a day assumed from the 1951 table, which lies outside this span), not sourced for 1895-1946.
sources: Segment-level: start 1895 per the reorganization date (Central of Georgia research file block [2]); 1901, 1903, 1915 and 1934 timetable anchors per Fowler GA route 40; end 1946 is an editorial abutment with cofg-nancy-hanks-ii (1947-1971), not an end of service; headway NOT SOURCED (estimate)
